output.decision: No—do not launch a multivariate hero × offer × checkout test this month. With 3,000 monthly sessions and a 2% baseline purchase conversion rate (about 60 purchases/month), splitting traffic across multiple combinations is unlikely to yield a timely, decision-ready result. Instead, select one highest-priority, low-risk change and run a sequential A/B test only after defining its hypothesis, guardrails, and measurement plan. This is an operational recommendation based on the supplied brand facts plus general experimentation practice; the library’s volume guidance is unverified and does not define a threshold.
next_steps: Choose one lever to test first—hero, offer, or checkout—using expected business impact, implementation risk, and reversibility.
Write a predefined hypothesis with a primary metric of revenue per session and guardrails such as conversion rate, average order value, refund rate, and checkout errors.
Estimate required sample size and expected runtime for a two-variant test before committing; defer if the runtime is not operationally acceptable.
Keep the other two experiences unchanged so the result is interpretable; do not stack overlapping tests on the same customer journey.
QA the selected variant repeatedly across devices, traffic sources, cart states, discount logic, payment methods, and analytics events before launch.
missing_inputs: Number of variants proposed for each of hero, offer, and checkout, plus the exact experiences.
Expected effect size or minimum detectable lift, desired confidence/power, and maximum acceptable test duration.
Revenue per session, average order value, margin impact, and discount/offer cost.
Whether checkout changes require platform, payment, legal, or promotional approvals and what tracking events are available.

evidence_used.supports: The supplied source advises using multivariate testing only at high volume, while leaving the threshold undefined.
The supplied source describes a practitioner’s sample-sizing practice of 50,000–100,000 sessions per test, dependent on placement; it is not presented as a universal rule.
The supplied source recommends a clear, predefined, measurable hypothesis.
The supplied source recommends repeated QA before a test goes live.
The supplied source recommends revenue per session or visitor rather than conversion rate alone.

assumptions: Monthly sessions and baseline conversion are representative of the planned test period.
A multivariate test would divide traffic among more than two combinations and seek purchase/revenue outcomes.
No major seasonal campaign or traffic increase will materially change available volume this month.
Tracking being validated means assignment, purchase, and revenue events can be measured reliably.
